rows.raw: {"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"replace","path":"sections[1].points[0]","value":"Limit correction to 10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours (and ~8 mEq/L per 24 hours thereafter); use a stricter 8 mEq/L/24h ceiling in high-risk patients [1]"},{"op":"append","path":"sections[1].points","value":"Chronic/asymptomatic SIADH: fluid restriction is first-line; if inadequate add oral urea or salt tablets with a loop diuretic, reserving vasopressin antagonists for selected monitored patients"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Severe symptoms (seizures, obtundation) get prompt 3% saline boluses (e.g. 150 mL over 20 min, repeatable) targeting only a ~5 mEq/L rise to break the emergency"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Chronic SIADH is managed with fluid restriction first, then urea or salt plus a loop diuretic; vasopressin antagonists are second-line and avoided in liver disease"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"High-risk-for-ODS patients (alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, advanced liver disease) need the tightest correction limits and frequent Na checks"}]}

rows.raw: {"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"replace","path":"sections[1].points[1]","value":"Start dapagliflozin 10 mg daily (or empagliflozin 10 mg daily) irrespective of diabetes status"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the fourth pillar: start if K+ <5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Check K+ and creatinine 1-2 weeks after starting or up-titrating an MRA, ARNI, or ACEi"},{"op":"append","path":"sections","value":{"heading":"Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["Aldosterone drives sodium retention, potassium/magnesium wasting, and myocardial fibrosis independent of ACEi/ARB effect","Spironolactone 12.5-25 mg daily or eplerenone 25 mg daily, titrated to 50 mg daily as tolerated","Initiate only if K+ <5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2; recheck K+ and creatinine within 1-2 weeks","Stop or reduce dose if K+ exceeds 5.5 mEq/L; avoid potassium supplements and NSAIDs"],"mechanism":"Blockade of aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor limits fibrosis and volume retention","teaching_pearl":"Gynecomastia is a spironolactone effect; switch to eplerenone rather than abandoning the pillar","board_tip":"RALES (spironolactone, NYHA III-IV) and EMPHASIS-HF (eplerenone, NYHA II) established the mortality benefit"}]}]

{"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"replace","path":"guideline_sources[1]","value":"2021 AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF Universal Definition and Classification of Heart Failure"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"HFimpEF requires a prior LVEF <=40%, a >=10-point absolute rise, and a follow-up LVEF >40%"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Guideline-directed therapy is continued indefinitely after EF improves, not tapered off"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"SGLT2 inhibitors benefit patients across the entire EF spectrum, including HFmrEF and HFpEF"},{"op":"replace","path":"visual_memory_card.bottom_right","value":"HFimpEF: prior EF <=40%, >=10-pt rise, now >40%"},{"op":"append","path":"sections","value":{"heading":"How classification drives therapy","minutes":"3-4 min","points":["HFrEF (EF <=40%): all four pillars - ARNI (preferred over ACE inhibitor or ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, or bisoprolol), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone), and an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)","HFmrEF (EF 41-49%): SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended; ARNI/ACEi/ARB, MRA, and beta-blocker carry weaker (2b) recommendations, with greatest benefit at the lower end of the EF range","HFpEF (EF >=50%): SGLT2 inhibitor recommended; MRA and ARNI may be considered, plus diuretics for congestion and aggressive treatment of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and obesity","HFimpEF: continue the full regimen that produced the improvement - TRED-HF showed relapse when therapy was withdrawn"],"mechanism":"Trial enrollment EF cutoffs, not pathophysiology, determine which drugs have proven benefit in each band","teaching_pearl":"Check the potassium and creatinine before starting an MRA - generally avoid initiating if K+ >5.0 mEq/L or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2","board_tip":"Do not withdraw GDMT for a normalized EF; the correct answer is to continue therapy and follow serial imaging"}}]}

{"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"replace","path":"summary_points[1]","value":"Long-term oxygen therapy improves survival only in severe chronic resting hypoxemia (PaO2 <=55 mmHg, or <=59 mmHg with cor pulmonale/polycythemia); it does not prolong survival in moderate desaturation, and smoking cessation is the other intervention with a clear mortality benefit"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Acute therapy: short-acting bronchodilators, prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, and antibiotics for selected exacerbations (increased sputum purulence plus increased dyspnea or volume, or need for ventilatory support)"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"NIV is first-line for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH <=7.35 with PaCO2 >45 mmHg) and reduces intubation, length of stay, and mortality"},{"op":"replace","path":"sections[1].points[1]","value":"Chronic azithromycin reduces exacerbation frequency in selected patients, best evidence in former smokers with exacerbations despite optimized inhaled therapy [2]"}]}

{"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"replace","path":"sections[0].points[2]","value":"Send the initial potassium before starting insulin: hold the infusion if K is <3.3 mEq/L and replace potassium first, since insulin will drive it lower"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Isotonic crystalloid comes first and itself lowers glucose substantially before any insulin is given"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Add dextrose to the fluids when glucose falls below ~200 mg/dL so the insulin infusion can continue until the gap closes"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Overlap the insulin infusion with subcutaneous basal insulin for 1-2 hours before stopping it to prevent rebound ketoacidosis"},{"op":"append","path":"sections","value":{"heading":"Resolution and transition","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["Resolution requires glucose <200 mg/dL plus two of: serum bicarbonate >=15 mEq/L, venous pH >7.3, anion gap <=12","Do not use glucose alone as the endpoint - add dextrose to the fluids when glucose falls below ~200 mg/dL and continue insulin at a lower rate until the gap closes","Give subcutaneous basal insulin 1-2 hours before stopping the drip; stopping the infusion without overlap causes rebound ketoacidosis"],"mechanism":"Ketogenesis is suppressed by continuous insulin exposure, not by normoglycemia, so the infusion must outlast the hyperglycemia","teaching_pearl":"Treat the gap, not the glucose","board_tip":"Persistent hyperchloremic non-gap acidosis after gap closure is expected from saline resuscitation and needs no further insulin"}}]}

{"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Confirm true hypotonic hyponatremia first — measure serum osmolality to exclude pseudohyponatremia (severe hyperlipidemia, paraproteinemia) and translocational causes (hyperglycemia, mannitol)"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg means ADH is appropriately suppressed (primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low solute intake); >100 mOsm/kg implies ongoing ADH action (SIADH, hypovolemia, heart failure, cirrhosis, thiazides)"},{"op":"replace","path":"sections[1].points[1]","value":"Severely symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, obtundation) warrants prompt 3% hypertonic saline: 150 mL IV over 20 minutes, repeated until the sodium rises ~5 mEq/L or symptoms resolve"},{"op":"append","path":"sections[1].points","value":"For chronic SIADH, fluid restriction is first-line; add oral urea or salt tablets with a loop diuretic if restriction fails — the 2014 European guideline advises against vasopressin receptor antagonists"}]}

{"verdict":"corrected","patches":[{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are a pillar, not a last resort: start if K+ <5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >=30 mL/min/1.73 m2, then recheck K+ and creatinine within 1-2 weeks"},{"op":"append","path":"summary_points","value":"Titrate each agent toward the trial-proven target dose or the maximally tolerated dose rather than leaving all four at initiation doses"},{"op":"append","path":"sections","value":{"heading":"MRA and putting the four pillars together","minutes":"3-4 min","points":["Spironolactone 12.5-25 mg daily or eplerenone 25 mg daily; MRA blocks aldosterone-mediated fibrosis, sodium retention and potassium/magnesium wasting","Requires K+ <5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >=30 mL/min/1.73 m2 before initiation; hold or stop if K+ >5.5 mEq/L","Recheck potassium and creatinine within 1-2 weeks of starting or up-titrating, then periodically","Sequence is flexible: begin low doses of several classes early and up-titrate every 1-2 weeks as blood pressure, renal function and potassium allow","Reserve loop diuretics for congestion and symptom relief; they do not confer the mortality benefit the four pillars do"],"mechanism":"Aldosterone blockade limits fibrosis and electrolyte losses, completing quadruple neurohormonal and metabolic therapy","teaching_pearl":"A modest asymptomatic creatinine rise or soft blood pressure is usually a titration problem, not a reason to abandon a pillar","board_tip":"Gynecomastia is a spironolactone effect; switch to eplerenone, which is far more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor"}}]}
